title: The danger of pleasure and the pagan defense of shows
english: Servants of God, understand the state of faith, the principle of truth, and the rule of discipline that, among the other errors of the world, also takes away the pleasures of the shows. You who are now drawing near to God, recognize it. You who have already testified and confessed that you have drawn near, recognize it, so that no one sins through ignorance or through pretending not to know. For the force of pleasures is so great that it both prolongs ignorance into an occasion for sin and corrupts conscience into pretense.

Against both of these, perhaps the opinions of pagans still flatter some people. In this matter they are accustomed to argue against us in this way: they say that such great comforts for the eyes and ears from outside do not obstruct religion in the mind and conscience, and God is not offended by the amusement of a person, since enjoying it at its proper time and in its proper place, with fear and honor toward God preserved, is not a crime.

But this is exactly what we are preparing to demonstrate: how these things do not belong to true religion and true obedience toward the true God. There are some who think that Christians, a race ready for death, are trained to this obstinacy by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they may more easily despise life once its reins, so to speak, have been cut away, and may not desire what they have already made superfluous for themselves. In this way it is supposed to be determined by human planning and foresight rather than by divine command. Of course it was irksome even for those who persevere in such great pleasures to die for the Lord. And yet, even if it were so, only with so fitting a plan did the obstinacy of discipline owe obedience.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by addressing fellow Christians and stating that the pleasures of the shows must be taken away from them, before quoting the pagan objection that such pleasures do not offend God.

title: God made all things, but the devil corrupted their uses
english: But now everyone puts forward this argument: all things were established by God and given to man, as we proclaim, and are certainly good, as all things of a good author are. Among these are reckoned all those things from which the shows are constructed—the horse, for example, and the lion, and the strength of bodies and the sweetness of voices. Therefore, they say, what consists of God's own creation can seem neither foreign nor hostile to God, nor should it be counted against God's worshippers, since it is not hostile to him, because it is not foreign.

And indeed the very structures of the places—the stones, the cement, the marbles, the columns—are God's things, for he gave them for the furnishing of the earth. But the very performances themselves take place under God's sky.

How wise an arguer human ignorance seems to itself, especially when it fears losing something of this kind from the joys and fruits of the world. In fact you will find more people whom the danger of pleasure rather than the danger of life calls away from this sect. For even a fool does not fear death as something owed, but even a wise man does not despise pleasure as something desired, since for both fool and wise man there is no other charm of life than pleasure.

No one denies, because no one is ignorant of what nature freely suggests, that God is the founder of the universe and that this universe is as good as it is handed over to man. But because they do not know God deeply except by natural law, not also by intimate acquaintance—from afar, not from near—they must necessarily be ignorant of how he commands or forbids the things he established to be administered, and at the same time what hostile rival force exists in opposition for adulterating the uses of the divine creation. For you cannot know either the will or the adversary of one whom you know less.

Therefore not only this must be considered: by whom all things were established, but also by whom they were perverted. For thus it will appear for what use they were established, if it appears for what use they were not. There is a great difference between corruption and integrity, because there is a great distance between the founder and the corrupter.

Besides, all the kinds of evils which even the pagans both forbid and defend as undoubted consist of the works of God. You see homicide accomplished by iron, by poison, by magic bindings: iron is as much God's thing as herbs are, as the angels are. Did the author, however, provide these things for the killing of man? On the contrary, he abolishes every kind of homicide with one primary command: "You shall not kill" (Exodus 20:13).

Likewise, who placed gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and whatever material is sought for fabricating idols in the world except God, the author of the world? Did he, however, provide that these things should be worshipped against himself? On the contrary, idolatry is the highest offense in his sight. What is there that is not God's, that offends God? But when it offends, it ceases to be God's, and when it ceases, it offends.

Man himself, the author of all outrages, is not only the work of God but also his image; and yet he has fallen away from his founder in both body and spirit. For we did not receive eyes for desire, and a tongue for evil speaking, and ears for receiving evil speaking, and a throat for the crime of the throat, and a belly for the partnership of gluttony, and genitals for the excesses of unchastity, and hands for violence, and feet for a wandering life; nor was the spirit placed in the body to become a deviser of plots, of frauds, of iniquities. I do not think so.

For if God, the exactor of innocence, hates all malignity and even all devised malice, then undoubtedly whatever he created he did not create for the ruin of the works he condemns, even though those same works are administered through the things he created—since this is the whole reason for condemnation: the perverse use of creation by created things.

We, therefore, who have known the Lord and have also seen his adversary, who have discovered the founder and have likewise caught the corrupter, ought neither to wonder nor to doubt: since that force, the corrupter and rival angel, cast down man himself—the work and image of God, the possessor of the whole universe—from his integrity from the beginning, it likewise changed the entire substance of his creation, established for integrity together with him, into perversity together with him against the founder, so that in the very creation granted to man and not to himself, he might both make man guilty before God and establish his own dominion.
orientation: Tertullian is answering the pagan objection that since God created everything used in the shows, the shows cannot be alien or hostile to God.

title: Scripture implicitly forbids the shows
english: Armed with this knowledge against the opinions of pagans, let us turn instead to the objections of our own people. For some of them, whose faith is either too simple or too scrupulous, demand scriptural authority for giving up shows, and they place themselves in uncertainty because abstinence of this kind is not denounced to God's servants specifically and by name.

Of course we nowhere find it laid down as openly as "You shall not kill, you shall not worship an idol, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit fraud" (Exodus 20:13-15), so explicitly defined: "You shall not go into the circus, you shall not go into the theater, you shall not watch a contest or a gladiatorial show."

But we do find that the first voice of David applies to this very category: "Blessed is the man," he says, "who has not gone into the council of the impious, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of ruin" (Psalm 1:1). For even if he seems to have proclaimed that righteous man blessed because he did not share in the council and assembly of the Jews who were plotting the death of the Lord, divine Scripture is nevertheless always applied broadly: wherever discipline is also strengthened according to the sense of the present matter, so that here too the voice is not foreign to the prohibition of shows.

For if David called a few Jews of that time a council of the impious, how much more is the vast assembly of the pagan people such a council? Are pagans less impious, less sinners, less enemies of Christ than the Jews of that time were? What of the fact that the other details also fit? For at the shows people sit in a chair and stand in a way; they call the walkways and the dividing barriers around the circuit and the separations of the common people along the slope "ways," and the place itself in the curve for sitting is also called a "chair."

Therefore let us understand the reverse statement as spoken generally: "Unhappy is he who has gone into any council of the impious, and has stood in any way of sinners, and has sat in any chair of ruin." Since it can also be interpreted specifically, it certainly admits of that. For certain pronouncements made specifically also have a general sense. When God admonishes the Israelites for discipline or rebukes them, he certainly addresses everyone; when he threatens destruction to Egypt and Ethiopia, he certainly judges beforehand against every sinful nation.
orientation: Tertullian is answering Christians who want an explicit scriptural prohibition of the shows, and he turns to Psalm 1 as a broad principle that covers them.

title: From the general principle to the baptismal renunciation
english: Egypt and Ethiopia stand for every sinful nation, from the particular to the whole kind. In the same way, every show is a council of the impious, from the whole kind to the particular.

So that no one thinks I am splitting hairs, I will turn to the principal authority of our seal of faith itself. When we enter the water and profess the Christian faith in the words of its law, we testify with our own mouth that we have renounced the devil, the devil's pomp, and his angels. What will be the highest and most outstanding thing in which the devil, the devil's pomp, and his angels are reckoned, if not idolatry? Every unclean and wicked spirit, if I may put it that way, since I will not dwell on it longer, is reckoned in idolatry. Therefore, if it has been established that the entire apparatus of the shows consists of idolatry, it will without doubt have been judged beforehand that our renunciation in the washing also extends to the shows. For the shows have been handed over to the devil, the devil's pomp, and his angels, namely through idolatry. I will call to mind the origins of each of them, in what cradles they grew up in the world; then the titles of certain ones, by what names they are called; then their apparatus, with what superstitions they are furnished; then the places, to what presiding deities they are dedicated; then the arts, to what authors they are assigned. If any of these does not pertain to an idol, it will pertain neither to idolatry nor to our abjuration.
orientation: Tertullian has just shown that Scripture's general condemnations include specific cases, and now turns to the authority of the baptismal renunciation itself.

title: The origin of the games traced to idolatry
english: The origins of the games are more obscure and unknown to most of our people, so I had to investigate them from the records of pagan literature. Many authors have published commentaries on this subject. This is how the origin of the games is handed down. Timaeus, the Greek historian, reports that Lydians from Asia, migrants under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, settled in Etruria after Tyrrhenus ceded the throne to his brother following a dispute over rule. So in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, they also instituted shows under the name of religion. From there the Romans summoned the performers and borrowed the occasion, the announcement, and the name, so that they were called ludii from the Lydians. But even though Varro, the Roman scholar, interprets ludii from ludus, that is, from play, just as they also called the Luperci ludii because they run about in play, he still counts that play of young men among festival days, temples, and religious observances. But no more about the cause of the word, since the cause of the thing is idolatry. For when the games were called Liberalia without distinction, they clearly proclaimed the honor of Father Bacchus. They were first performed for Bacchus by country folk because of the benefit they attribute to him, the gift of wine. Then the games were called Consualia, which at first honored Neptune. They call the same god Consus as well.

Next, Romulus instituted the Equirria for Mars, named from the horses. Although some also defend the Consualia as Romulus's, because he dedicated them to Consus, the god whom they call the god of counsel. That counsel, of course, was the one by which he devised the rape of the Sabine women as wives for his soldiers. A plainly upright counsel, so-called, and even now among the Romans themselves just and lawful. I will not say in the sight of God. This too contributes to the stain of the origin, so that you should not think good what took its beginning from evil, from shamelessness, from violence, from hatred, from a fratricidal founder, from a son of Mars. And even now there is an altar to that Consus sunk in the circus at the first turning posts, underground, with an inscription of this sort: 'Consus in council, Mars in war, the Lares powerful.' Public priests sacrifice at it on the Nones of July, and the Flamen Quirinalis and the Vestal Virgins on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. After this, the same Romulus instituted games for Jupiter Feretrius on the Tarpeian, which Piso records were called the Tarpeian and Capitoline games. After him Numa Pompilius made games for Mars and Robigo, for they also invented a goddess of blight. Then Tullus Hostilius, then Ancus Martius, and the rest. Which of them instituted games for which idols and in what order is set down in Suetonius Tranquillus, or in the sources from which Tranquillus received it. But this will be enough to establish the guilt of the origin in idolatry.
orientation: Tertullian is beginning his argument that the shows are rooted in idolatry by tracing their historical origins from pagan sources.

title: Titles of the games reveal their idolatrous origin
english: Later generations add their own testimony to that of antiquity. Even in the titles of the present age they display the pattern of the origin, for the titles mark to which idol and to which superstition the games of each kind were assigned. The Megalensian and Apollinarian games are celebrated publicly, and likewise the Cerealian, Neptunalian, Latin, and Floralian games. The remaining games have their grounds in superstition: the birthdays and solemnities of kings, public prosperities, and municipal festivals. Among these, bequests also perform funeral rites for the memories of private individuals, and this too follows the antiquity of the institution. For from the beginning games were reckoned in two ways: sacred and funereal, that is, for the gods of the nations and for the dead.

But as far as we are concerned, it makes no difference to the charge of idolatry under what name or title they are held, as long as they reach the same spirits whom we renounce. Let them hold them for the dead; let them hold them for their gods. They do for their dead just as they do for their gods. One condition belongs to each part: one idolatry, one renunciation of ours against idolatry.
orientation: Tertullian has just shown that the first Roman games were instituted for idols, and now he argues that the names and occasions of later games continue to mark them as idolatrous.

title: Common origin and apparatus of the games
english: The games of both kinds, then, have a common origin, and their titles are common, since their causes are common. So their apparatus must also be common, because of the general guilt of the idolatry that gave them birth.

But the display of the circus is somewhat more ostentatious, and to it belongs this name in a special sense: the parade that goes before. This parade proves what it is in itself from the row of images, from the procession of statues, from the chariots, the sacred wagons, the covered carriages, the thrones, the crowns, the spoils.

How many sacred rites besides, how many sacrifices go before, come between, and follow after; how many colleges, how many priesthoods, how many offices are set in motion—the people of Rome know, where the assembly of demons has settled.

If these things are administered with less care in the provinces because of smaller resources, still all circuses everywhere must be assigned to that source from which they are sought; let them be traced back to the place from which they are taken. For a thin stream from its own source, and a modest shoot from its own foliage, retains the quality of its origin.

Let ambition or frugality see to what the parade's character is. Any parade of the circus, whatever its quality, offends God: even if it carries around few images, in one there is idolatry; even if it draws one sacred wagon, it is still Jupiter's chariot. Any idolatry, however meanly equipped or modestly wealthy, is splendid in the wealth of its own crime.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that both sacred and funereal games share one idolatrous origin, and now turns to the common apparatus of the games, especially the more ostentatious parade of the circus.

title: The circus as a place full of idols
english: Now let me continue with the places, as I proposed. The circus is chiefly consecrated to the Sun. Its temple stands in the middle of the space, and the Sun's image shines out from the temple's pediment, because they did not think that one whom they keep in the open should be consecrated under a roof. They claim that the first show was put on by Circe for the Sun, her father, as they would have it, and from her they derive the name of the circus. Clearly a sorceress certainly did business for them under this name, for the demons and angels whose priestess she was. How many idolatries, then, do you recognize in the appearance of that place? Each ornament of the circus is a separate temple. The eggs they assign to the honor of Castor and Pollux, those who are not ashamed to believe they were born from a swan, from Jupiter. They cast forth dolphins to Neptune. The columns bear images of Sessia from the sowings, Messia from the harvests, Tutulina from the protection of fruits. Before them three altars serve three gods: the Great, the Powerful, the Strong. They consider these to be the Samothraces. The hugeness of the obelisk, as Hermateles affirms, is debased to the Sun. Its inscription, and from it its tribute, is superstition from Egypt. The assembly of demons was incomplete without its own Great Mother; so she presides there over the canal. Consus, as we said, is hidden underground at the turning posts; Murcia is there too. He made even them into an idol: they claim Murcia is a goddess of love, to whom they dedicated a temple in that part. Take note, Christian, how many unclean names have taken possession of the circus. Foreign to you is the religion that so many spirits of the devil have occupied.

Now is the place to discuss the places themselves, to forestall some people's question. "What then," you say, "if I go to the circus at some other time, will I be endangered by its defilement?" There is no prescription about places. For not only these meeting-places of the shows, but even the temples themselves, a servant of God can enter without danger to his discipline when a simple cause compels him, provided only that it does not pertain to the business or function proper to that place. Besides, the streets and the forum and the baths and the inns and our very houses are not entirely without idols: Satan and his angels have filled the whole world. Yet it is not because we are in the world that we fall away from God, but if we touch any of the world's crimes. Therefore if I enter the Capitol or the Serapeum as a sacrificer or worshiper, I shall fall away from God, just as I would as a spectator at the circus or theater. Places do not defile us by themselves, but the things done in them, by which we have argued the places themselves are defiled. From the defiled we are defiled.
orientation: Tertullian is now examining the places where the shows are held, arguing that the circus itself is consecrated to the Sun and filled with idols.

title: The chariot and its colors are demonic inventions
english: We recall the places so named for this reason: to show that what happens in them belongs to the beings for whom the places themselves are named.

Now for the art by which the circus shows are presented. Riding was once a simple matter. A man rode on the horse's back, and it was ordinary, everyday use. It was no crime. But when riding was forced into the games, it passed from a gift of God into the service of demons.

So this kind of riding is assigned to Castor and Pollux. The Greek poet Stesichorus teaches that their horses were distributed to them by Mercury. Neptune too is a god of horses; the Greeks call him Hippios, the Horseman. They consecrated the single-horse chariot to Jupiter, the four-horse chariot to the Sun, and the two-horse chariot to the Moon.

Erichthonius was the first who dared to yoke four horses to a chariot and stand victorious on swift wheels. Now Erichthonius, the son of Minerva and Vulcan, born from lust that fell to the earth, is a demonic portent. Or rather, he is the devil himself, not a mere snake. If Trochilus the Argive is the inventor of the chariot, he dedicated his work to Juno first. If Romulus first displayed a four-horse chariot at Rome, I think he too has been enrolled among the idols, if he is the same as Quirinus.

With such founders the four-horse chariots were produced, and rightly the charioteers clothed themselves in the colors of idolatry. For at first there were only two colors, white and red. White was vowed to winter because of the white snows, red to summer because of the sun's redness. But later, as much by pleasure as by superstition, they advanced further. Some consecrated red to Mars, others white to the West Winds, green to Mother Earth or to spring, and blue to Sky and Sea or to autumn.
But since every kind of idolatry has been condemned by God, certainly that too is condemned which is profaned by the elements of the world.
orientation: Tertullian is tracing the origins of the circus, now turning from the places to the art of chariot-racing itself.

title: Theater as shared property of Venus and Bacchus
english: Let us now turn to theatrical matters. We have already shown that the theater shares its origin with the games, and that its titles are equal to theirs, since from the beginning the very name and administration of the games were joined with the equestrian affair. Its apparatus is also a partner from that side, since the way to the stage leads from temples and altars and that unhappy business of incense and blood, amid flutes and trumpets, under two most polluted arbiters of funerals and sacrifices: the dissignator, who arranges the funeral procession, and the haruspex, who inspects the entrails of sacrificial victims. So when we passed from the origins of the games to the circus, we will now direct our course from there to the theatrical games.

Because of the vice of its location, the theater is properly a shrine of Venus. This is how that kind of work finally emerged into the world. For often the censors were destroying theaters just as they were being born, since they foresaw the immense danger from their wantonness. So here already the pagans' own judgment may serve as testimony, agreeing with us and giving us, for the heightening of discipline, even a human prerogative. And so Pompey the Great, lesser than his theater alone, when he had built that citadel of every foulness, fearing at some point the censorial censure of his memory, placed a temple of Venus on top and, calling the people to the dedication by edict, named it not a theater but a temple of Venus. 'Under it,' he said, 'we have placed the steps for the shows.' Thus he covered a work condemned and still to be condemned with the title of a temple, and mocked discipline with superstition.

But Venus and Bacchus are well matched. Those two demons are conspirators and sworn allies of drunkenness and lust. Therefore the theater of Venus is also the house of Bacchus. For they used to call other theatrical games properly Liberalia, devoted to Bacchus beyond the rest—those which among the Greeks are Dionysia, also instituted by Bacchus. And clearly in the theatrical arts too there is the patronage of Bacchus and Venus. The things that are private and proper to the stage—gesture and the bending of the body—they sacrifice to the softness of Venus and Bacchus, dissolved through sex and through extravagance. But the things carried out by voice and melody and instruments and writings have Apollos, Muses, Minervas, and Mercuries as their servants. Hate, O Christian, the things whose authors you cannot help but hate.

Now we want to speak about the arts and about those whose authors we curse in their names. We know that the names of the dead are nothing, just as their images themselves are nothing; but we are not ignorant of who operates under those names and instituted images, and rejoices and feigns divinity—namely worthless spirits, demons. We see therefore that even the arts are dedicated to the honors of those who inhabit the names of their authors, and that they are not free from idolatry, since their founders are for that very reason considered gods. Indeed, as far as the arts are concerned, we ought to have understood more deeply that the demons from the beginning, foreseeing for themselves among the other pollutions of idolatry also the defilements of the shows, by which they might call man away from the Lord and bind him to their own honor, inspired the talents of such arts as well. For what was going to come to them would not have been procured by others, nor would they have published it through other men then than through those very ones in whose names and images and histories they determined to carry out for themselves the business of the deceit of consecration. So that the order may be completed, let us also enter upon a review of the contests.
orientation: Tertullian has just traced the circus and chariot racing to idolatrous founders, and now turns to the theater, arguing that its very location, titles, and arts belong to Venus and Bacchus.

title: The origins and idolatrous apparatus of the contests
english: The games themselves take their origin from this nearness to idolatry. That is why they were instituted either as sacred or as funerary, and are performed for the gods of the nations or for the dead. The titles tell the same story: the Olympian games for Jupiter, the ones at Rome called the Capitoline, likewise the Nemean for Hercules, the Isthmian for Neptune, and the various contests for other dead men.

What wonder, then, if the very apparatus of the contests is defiled by idolatry: by the profane crowns, by the priestly presidents, by the ministers of the guilds of the gods, and finally by the very blood of oxen?

To complete the point about the common place: in place of the guild of the musical arts, the arts of Minerva, and the arts of Apollo, and also the arts of Mars, they compete through combat and through the trumpet in the stadium. The stadium itself is certainly a temple of that idol whose solemnities it celebrates.
But the gymnastic arts as well were handed down by the disciplines of the Castors and the Herculeses and the Mercuries.
orientation: Tertullian is completing his review of the origins of the shows by turning from the arts to the contests themselves, showing that their titles, equipment, places, and disciplines all belong to pagan gods.

title: The amphitheater's origin in death-offerings and its demonic consecration
english: It remains to examine that most famous and most popular show. The gladiatorial show takes its name from duty, since the Latin word for the show, munus, also means a duty or gift. The ancients believed they were performing a duty to the dead with this spectacle, after they had softened it with a semblance of humanity. For in early times, since it was believed that the souls of the dead were appeased by human blood, they bought captives or slaves of poor standing and sacrificed them at the funerals. Later it pleased them to veil their impiety with pleasure. So they trained those they had acquired in whatever arms they could and however they could, just enough to learn how to be killed, and soon on the appointed day of the offerings to the dead they dispatched them at the tombs. In this way they consoled death with murders. This is the origin of the gladiatorial show. But gradually they advanced to as much favor as cruelty, because the pleasure of the holidays was not satisfied unless human bodies were torn apart by wild beasts as well. What was offered to the dead, then, was assigned to the cult of the dead. This kind of thing is idolatry, since idolatry is also a kind of cult of the dead: both the one and the other serve the dead. And in the idols of the dead, demons dwell.

Consider also the titles. Even though this kind of exhibition has passed from honors for the dead to honors for the living—I mean the political offices under which such shows were given, the quaestorships and magistracies and priesthoods of the flamens and priestly offices—since the dignity of the name is still held by the charge of idolatry, whatever is administered under the name of that dignity must necessarily share in the stains of the source from which it has its causes. We will interpret the apparatus in the same way, as things assigned to the display of those very honors: the purple robes, the rods of office, the fillets, the crowns, and finally the assemblies and edicts and the sacrificial cakes offered on the eve of the games are not without the devil's pomp, not without the invitation of demons.

Why should I speak at length about that dreadful place, which even perjuries cannot endure? For the amphitheater is consecrated with more numerous and harsher names than the Capitol: it is a temple of all demons. As many unclean spirits settle there as the place holds people. And to conclude about the arts as well, we know that Mars and Diana preside over each of the two games.
orientation: Tertullian is completing his survey of the shows' idolatrous elements by examining the gladiatorial show, its origin in funeral sacrifices, and the amphitheater as a temple of all demons.

title: Idols are nothing, but what pagans do they do to demons
english: I think we have now filled out the full account of how many and what kinds of ways the shows commit idolatry—in their origins, their titles, their apparatus, their places, their arts—so that we may be certain that they in no respect belong to us, who have renounced idols twice over. Not that an idol is anything, as the apostle says (1 Corinthians 8:4), but because the things they do, they do for demons—demons who dwell in the consecrations of idols, whether of the dead or of those they think are gods. Therefore, since both kinds of idols share one condition, since the dead and the gods are one and the same, we abstain from both idolatries. We spit upon temples no less than tombs. We acknowledge neither altar, we worship neither image, we do not sacrifice, we do not make offerings. Nor do we eat from what has been sacrificed or offered, because we cannot eat the meal of God and the meal of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). If then we free our gullet and belly from defilements, how much more do we abstain from idol-sacrificed and dead-sacrificed pleasures in our more august parts—our ears and our eyes? Those pleasures are not passed through the intestines but are digested in the spirit and the soul itself, whose cleanness matters more to God than that of the intestines.
orientation: Tertullian has just finished cataloguing how the shows commit idolatry in their origins, titles, apparatus, places, and arts, and now grounds the Christian abstention in the nature of idolatry itself.

title: The general condemnation of desire covers shows
english: Now that I have brought in the name of idolatry, which alone should be enough as a ground for rejecting the shows, let me argue the matter from another angle, out of abundance. I do this especially for those who flatter themselves that this abstinence is not specifically prescribed. As if too little is pronounced against the shows when the desires of the world are condemned. For just as there is desire of money, of rank, of appetite, of lust, or of glory, so too there is desire of pleasure; and the kinds of pleasure are also shows. I think that desires, when named generally, contain pleasures within themselves; and pleasures, when understood equally generally, are discussed specifically in the shows as well.
orientation: Tertullian has just argued that Christians abstain from idolatrous pleasures in their ears and eyes, and now turns to a further argument for those who claim no specific prohibition of shows exists.

title: The passions of the shows are incompatible with the Holy Spirit
english: I have already discussed the condition of the places: they do not defile us by themselves, but by what is done in them. Once they have drunk in that defilement, they then spit it back onto others. So let the principal title, idolatry, see to it, as we have said. Let us bring the remaining qualities of those things against all the gods.

God has commanded that the Holy Spirit—tender and delicate as it is by the goodness of its nature—be handled with tranquility, gentleness, quiet, and peace, not disturbed by frenzy, bile, anger, or grief. How can this possibly agree with the shows? Every show involves a shaking of the spirit. Where there is pleasure, there is also eagerness, through which pleasure has its savor. Where there is eagerness, there is also rivalry, through which eagerness has its savor. And where there is rivalry, there is frenzy, bile, anger, grief, and the rest of what follows from these—none of which is suitable for discipline.

Even if someone enjoys the shows modestly and uprightly, according to his rank, age, or natural disposition, his mind is still moved, and not without a silent passion of the spirit. No one comes to pleasure without feeling; no one suffers feeling without its own lapses. Those very lapses are the incitements of feeling. If feeling ceases, there is no pleasure, and the man is already guilty of vanity by going where he gains nothing. But I think vanity too is foreign to us.

What of the fact that he judges himself by sitting among those whose detester he confesses himself to be, even unwillingly? It is not enough for us if we ourselves do no such thing, unless we also do not associate with those who do such things. "If you saw a thief," it says, "you ran together with him." Would that we did not even linger in the world with them! But still, in worldly matters we are separated, because the world is God's, but worldly things are the devil's.
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that the shows must be rejected because they excite passions contrary to Christian discipline, even apart from their idolatrous origins.

title: The circus is the seat of fury, and Christians are removed from it
english: So when fury is forbidden to us, we are removed from every show, even from the circus, where fury properly presides. Look at the crowd coming to that show already with fury, already disorderly, already blind, already stirred up about bets. The praetor is too slow for them; their eyes are always rolling with the lots in his urn. Then they hang anxiously on the signal, and there is one voice of one madness. Recognize the madness from its vanity: "He's off," they say, and they tell each other what everyone has seen at the same moment. I have here the evidence of their blindness: they do not see what has been thrown. They think it is the starting cloth, but it is the figure of the devil cast down from on high. From that, then, they go into furies and passions and quarrels and everything not permitted to priests of peace. From there come curses and insults without any just cause for hatred, even applause without any deserving love. For what will those who act there gain for themselves, when they are not themselves? Unless perhaps this alone, through which they are not themselves: they are saddened by another's misfortune and rejoice at another's good fortune. Whatever they wish for, whatever they detest, is foreign to them; so their love is groundless and their hatred unjust. Or can it be permitted to love without cause any more than to hate without cause? God certainly forbids hatred even with cause, since He commands enemies to be loved; God does not allow cursing even with cause, since He commands those who curse to be blessed. But what is more bitter than the circus, where they do not even spare their rulers or their own citizens? If any of these things in which the circus rages is fitting for the saints anywhere, then it will also be permitted in the circus; but if nowhere, then not in the circus either.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that because fury is forbidden to Christians, they are removed from every show, and he now examines the circus as the place where fury properly presides.

title: The theater is condemned as a school of impurity
english: In the same way, we are commanded to put away all impurity. This is how we are separated from the theater as well. The theater is impurity's own council chamber, where nothing is approved except what is not approved anywhere else. Its highest charm is built up entirely from filth. Atellanus acts out that filth with gestures. The mime represents it even through women's roles, destroying the sense of sex and of modesty, so that people blush more easily at home than on stage. The pantomime suffers that filth in his body from boyhood, so that he can become an artist. Even the prostitutes themselves, the victims of public lust, are brought out on stage. They are more wretched in the presence of women, from whom alone they used to hide. They are paraded before the faces of every age and every rank. Their location, their price, their notice are proclaimed even to those who have no need of them. Even what should have hidden in darkness and in their own caves, to keep from contaminating the daylight, is proclaimed. I say nothing of the rest. Let the senate blush. Let all the orders blush. Let those very destroyers of their own modesty, terrified by their own gestures before the light and the people, blush once a year.

But if all impurity is to be abominated by us, why should it be lawful to hear what it is not lawful to speak? We know that even scurrility and every idle word is judged by God. Why should it be equally lawful to see what it is a crime to do? Why should the things that defile a person when brought out through the mouth not seem to defile a person when admitted through the ears and eyes? The ears and eyes are the spirit's attendants, and a person cannot be kept clean whose attendants are polluted. You have, then, the prohibition of the theater from the prohibition of impurity.

If we also reject the teaching of secular literature as counted foolishness before God, enough is prescribed for us concerning those kinds of shows that secular literature marks out as the playful or athletic stage. But if tragedies and comedies are bloody and wanton actresses of crimes and lusts, impious and extravagant, no remembrance of anything atrocious or vile is better. What is rejected in deed must not be received even in word.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that since Scripture forbids impurity, Christians are thereby separated from the theater, which is its private council-chamber.

title: The stadium's vanities and the devil's wrestling
english: But if you insist that the stadium is named in Scripture, you will certainly win your point. Yet you will not deny that what goes on in the stadium is unworthy of your eyes: punches, kicks, blows, every wantonness of the hand, and all the fighting done to the human face, which is the divine image. You will never approve of vain races and javelin throws and even vainer jumps. Nowhere will strength that is either injurious or vain please you. Nor will you care for an artificially built body, since it surpasses the molding of God, and you will hate men fattened for the leisure of Greece. And wrestling is the devil's business: the devil first threw down the first human beings. The boxing glove itself is a serpentine force, clinging to seize, twisting to bind, slippery to escape. You have no use for crowns; why do you hunt for pleasures from crowns?
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that each kind of show is condemned by Scripture, now turning from the theater to the stadium and its athletic contests.

title: The amphitheater cannot be defended even by punishment of the guilty
english: Should we now wait to seek from the Scriptures a repudiation of the amphitheater as well? If we can claim that savagery, impiety, and ferocity are permitted to us, let us go into the amphitheater. If we are what we are said to be, let us delight in human blood. It is good when the guilty are punished. Who but a guilty man will deny this? And yet even the innocent ought not to rejoice in another's punishment; rather, it befits the innocent to grieve that a man, his equal, has become so guilty that he is expended so cruelly. But who is my guarantor that the guilty are always condemned to the beasts or to whatever punishment, so that it is not also inflicted on innocence, whether through the vengeance of an unjust judge, the weakness of a defense, or the pressure of torture? How much better, then, not to know when the wicked are punished, lest I also know when the good perish—if the good are indeed wise. Certainly, innocent gladiators enter the games to become victims of public pleasure. Even those who are condemned to the games—what sort of correction is it that they advance from a lighter offense into murderers? But I have answered these points to the pagans. For the rest, far be it that a Christian should need longer instruction in turning away from this show. Although no one can express all these things more fully than one who still watches. I prefer not to fill my mind than to remember.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians about the amphitheater, continuing his argument that the shows are incompatible with Christian discipline.

title: God sees all, so no place or time excuses what he condemns
english: How empty, then—no, how desperate—is the argument of those who, no doubt to evade losing their pleasure, claim that the Scriptures nowhere mention this abstinence specifically or locally, nowhere directly forbid a servant of God to enter gatherings of this kind. I recently heard a new defense of a certain sweet amusement. A pagan objector says, "The sun—indeed even God himself—looks on from heaven and is not contaminated." True enough: the sun sends its rays into a sewer and is not defiled. But would that God looked on no crimes of men, so that we might all escape judgment! Yet he does look on robberies, and he looks on falsehoods and adulteries and frauds and idolatries and the shows themselves. And for that reason, then, we will not watch, lest we be seen by him who watches all things.

You compare, man, the accused and the judge—the accused, who is guilty because he is seen, and the judge, who is judge because he sees. Do we then pursue fury outside the limits of the circus, and aim at shamelessness outside the hinges of the theater, and insolence outside the stadium, and mercilessness outside the amphitheater, because God has eyes even outside the vaults and the steps and the awnings? We are mistaken: nowhere and never is what God condemns excused; nowhere and never is what is always and everywhere unlawful permitted. This is the integrity of truth, and the fullness of discipline owed to it, and the equality of fear and the faithfulness of obedience: not to change the sentence nor to vary the judgment. What is truly good or evil cannot be anything other than it is.
orientation: Tertullian is answering those who claim Scripture nowhere specifically forbids attending the shows, and he reports a recent objection that God himself looks on without being defiled.

title: Pagans' shifting standards of good and evil
english: But all things are fixed by the truth of God. Pagans possess no fullness of truth, because God is not their teacher of truth. They interpret good and evil according to their own whim and desire: what is good in one place is evil in another, and what is evil in one place is good in another.

So it happens that the same man who in public would barely lift his tunic out of necessity to relieve his bladder, in the circus strips off his clothing only to throw all his shame in the face of everyone. The man who guards his virgin daughter's ears from every obscene word himself leads her into the theater to hear those voices and see those gestures. The man who in the streets either breaks up or detests a brawl carried on by hand, in the stadium gives his vote to more serious fights. The man who shudders at the corpse of a person who died by the common law of nature, in the amphitheater leans over from above with most patient eyes upon bodies torn and scattered, and filthy in their own blood.

Indeed, the man who comes to the show to approve the punishment of a murderer, himself compels an unwilling gladiator to commit murder with whips and rods. And the man who demands a lion for some distinguished murderer, demands the wooden sword and the cap as a prize for a cruel gladiator. He also has the slain gladiator brought back so he can look at his face, more gladly recognizing up close the man he wanted killed from a distance, all the harsher if he did not succeed.
orientation: Tertullian is contrasting the fixed truth of God with the arbitrary moral judgments of pagans, showing how the same people behave inconsistently in public life and at the shows.

title: The perversity of honoring the art but disgracing the artist
english: What wonder is it? These are the uneven ways of men who mix and exchange the state of good and evil through inconstancy of feeling and variety of judgment. Indeed, the very authors and administrators of the shows, the charioteers, stage actors, athletes trained in the xystus, and arena fighters, those most beloved men for whom men lay down their souls and women even their bodies, for whose sake they commit themselves to the very things they condemn, these men they depose and diminish by the same art by which they magnify them. Indeed, they openly condemn them with disgrace and diminution of status, barring them from the senate house, the speaker's platform, the senate, the equestrian order, and all other honors and certain ornaments at once.

What perversity! They love those whom they punish; they degrade those whom they approve; they magnify the art and mark the artist. What kind of judgment is it, that a man should be darkened because of the very things through which he earns favor? Indeed, what a confession of an evil thing it is! The performers of these things, though they are most accepted, are not without a mark.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the shows are condemned even by their own patrons, who love the performers yet strip them of civic honors.

title: Divine judgment on performers
english: Human memory itself, even when the clamor of pleasure protests, judges that such men deserve condemnation: stripped of the goods of their rank and cast onto a rock of notoriety. How much more, then, will divine justice take notice of artisans of this kind? Will that charioteer please God? He is the disturber of so many souls, the servant of so many furies. He is like a priest crowned or painted like a pimp, whom the devil adorned to be carried off in a chariot, unlike Elijah. Will the actor who changes his face with a razor please God? He is unfaithful to his own face. He is not content to make it resemble Saturn and Isis and Bacchus. On top of that, he exposes it to the insults of slaps, as if he were playing at the Lord's command. Of course the devil also teaches that the cheek to be struck should be offered patiently. So too he has lifted the tragic actors on buskins, because no one can add one cubit to his stature: he wants to make Christ a liar.

Now I ask whether the very work of masks pleases God, who forbids every likeness to be made. How much more the likeness of his own image? The author of truth does not love the false. Everything that is feigned is adultery with him. Therefore he will not approve a voice that lies about sex and age, that asserts loves, rages, groans, tears. For he condemns all hypocrisy. Moreover, when in the law he prescribes that cursed is he who will be clothed in women's garments, what will he judge of the pantomime, who is even bent into women's garments? Surely that artisan of blows will also go unpunished. For such scars of the boxing gloves and calluses of blows and cauliflower ears he received from God when he was formed. Therefore God lent him eyes, so that they might fail under the beating. I say nothing of the man who puts a human being in front of a lion, lest he be less a murderer than the one who afterwards cuts the same man's throat.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that if human judgment marks performers with disgrace, God's justice will condemn them even more, and he now lists the kinds of performers and their arts that cannot please God.

title: The logic of renunciation: what displeases God is the devil's pomp
english: How many ways have we now proved that nothing assigned to the shows is pleasing to God! But is what is not pleasing to God fitting for God's servant? If we have shown that all these things were instituted for the devil's sake and furnished from the devil's resources—for whatever is not God's or displeases God is nothing but the devil's—then this is the devil's pomp, against which we swore in the seal of faith. And what we have sworn against, we must not participate in by deed, word, sight, or gaze. Otherwise we swear against it and then rescind the seal by rescinding its testimony.

Does anything remain, then, but to demand an answer from the pagans themselves? Let them announce to us whether Christians are permitted to use the show. Yet it is precisely from the repudiation of shows that they recognize a Christian to have been made. So the one who destroys the mark by which he is recognized plainly denies it. What hope remains for such a person? No one crosses into the enemy's camp except by throwing away his own weapons, abandoning the standards and oaths of his own prince, and agreeing to perish at the same time.
orientation: Tertullian has just finished cataloguing the idolatrous and cruel arts of the shows and now draws the conclusion that Christians, having renounced the devil's pomp at baptism, must not participate in it in any way.

title: The impossibility of godly thought at the shows
english: Will he be thinking about God at that moment, seated where there is nothing of God? He will have peace in his soul, I suppose, while he is rooting for a charioteer, and he will learn modesty while he is spellbound by the mimes. No, in every show nothing will prove a greater stumbling block than the very care people take over their appearance, women and men alike. The mere fact of being together, the shared partisanship or the rivalry between them over their sexual commerce, fans the sparks of lusts. In short, no one entering a show thinks of anything first except being seen and seeing.

But while the tragic actor is shouting, will he be going over the exclamations of some prophet? Amid the measures of effeminate flute-players, will he be meditating on a psalm? And when the athletes are competing, will he be ready to say that a blow should not be struck back? Then he could also be reminded of mercy while he is riveted on the bites of bears and the sponges of the net-fighters. May God turn away from his own people so great a desire for destructive pleasure!

For what is it to go from the church of God into the church of the devil, from heaven, as they say, into the mire? To weary those hands you have lifted up to God by afterward applauding an actor? To give testimony to a gladiator from the mouth by which you have uttered 'Amen' over the Holy One, and to say 'forever and ever' to anyone at all other than God and Christ?
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians who attend the shows, asking whether they can possibly keep godly thoughts and conduct there.

title: Demons claim those who attend the shows
english: Why should I not also be open to demons of this kind? For an example occurred, with the Lord as witness, of a woman who went to the theater and returned from there with a demon. And so when the unclean spirit was being pressed in an exorcism because it had dared to attack a believer, it said firmly: "And I did it with good right: I found her in my own place." It is also established that a linen cloth was shown in a dream to another woman on the night of the day she had heard a tragedy, with the actor named in reproach, and that that woman died within five days. Certainly other cases have also come to light concerning those who, by sharing with the devil at the shows, have fallen from the Lord. For no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:24). What has light to do with darkness? What has life to do with death?
orientation: Tertullian is warning Christians that attending the shows hands them over to demons, and he now gives examples of demonic possession and death that followed such attendance.

title: Flee the gatherings where God is blasphemed
english: We ought to hate these gatherings and assemblies of pagans, if only because there the name of God is blasphemed, there the daily lions are demanded against us, from there persecutions are decreed, from there temptations are sent out. What will you do when you are singled out in that meeting-place of unholy votes? Not that you can suffer anything there from men, for no one knows you are a Christian, but consider what is happening to you in heaven. Do you doubt that at the very moment the devil rages against the church, all the angels look down from heaven and mark each person: who has spoken a blasphemy, who has listened, who has lent his tongue, who has lent his ears to the devil against God? Therefore you will not flee the seats of Christ's enemies, that chair of pestilences, and the very air above, befouled by wicked voices?

Let the shows be sweet, pleasing, and simple, even honorable in some respects. No one serves poison by itself, with gall and hellebore; he puts the evil into seasoned dishes, well flavored and mostly sweet. So too the devil steeps the deadly thing he makes in the things most pleasing and acceptable to God. Treat everything there, whether brave, honorable, loud, melodious, or subtle, as drops of honey from a poisoned little vessel, and do not make the gullet of pleasure worth as much as the danger that comes through sweetness.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing Christians directly, urging them to hate and avoid the public gatherings of pagans because there God is blasphemed and the devil works against the church.

title: The Christian's feast is not yet
english: Let his guests be fattened on such sweets: the places, the times, and the host are all his. Our dinner, our wedding, has not yet come. We cannot recline at table with them, because they cannot with us; the matter is arranged by turns. Now they rejoice, we struggle. "The world," Christ says, "will rejoice; you will be sad" (John 16:20). Let us mourn, then, while the pagans rejoice, so that when they begin to mourn, we may rejoice, lest by rejoicing together now, we also mourn together then.

You are delicate, Christian, if you desire pleasure even in this world; indeed you are far too foolish if you think that is pleasure. Certain philosophers gave this name to rest and tranquility; in that they rejoice, in that they are diverted, in that they even boast. You sigh for turning posts and stage and dust and sand. I would have you say: we cannot live without pleasure, we who must die with pleasure. For what other wish do we have than the apostles'—to depart from the world and be received with the Lord? Where the wish is, there is the pleasure.
orientation: Tertullian is contrasting the present joy of pagans at the shows with the deferred joy of Christians, who should mourn now so they may rejoice later.

title: Christian pleasures replace pagan shows
english: Do you really think you need this space for delights? Why are you so ungrateful that you do not count as enough the many great pleasures God has contributed to you, and do not even recognize them? What is more joyful than reconciliation with God the Father and Lord, than the revelation of truth, than the recognition of errors, than pardon for so many past crimes? What greater pleasure is there than disgust at pleasure itself, than contempt for the whole world, than true freedom, than a clean conscience, than a life that is sufficient, than no fear of death? What of trampling the gods of the nations, expelling demons, working cures, seeking revelations, living for God? These are the pleasures, these are the shows of Christians—holy, everlasting, free. In these, interpret the circus games for yourself: gaze at the course of the world, the slipping seasons, count out the laps already run, wait for the turning-post of the consummation, defend the fellowship of the churches, rise at God's signal, stand at the angel's trumpet, glory in the martyrs' palms. If the theater's teachings delight you, we have literature enough, verses enough, sayings enough, songs enough, voices enough—not fables but truths, not tricks but simplicities. Do you want boxing and wrestling too? They are at hand, and they are not small or few. Look at impurity thrown down by chastity, faithlessness slain by faith, cruelty crushed by mercy, wantonness overshadowed by modesty. Such are the contests among us, in which we ourselves win the crown. Do you want some blood as well? You have Christ's.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the Christian reader directly, urging them to find their entertainment in the spiritual blessings and moral victories of the Christian life rather than in the public shows.

title: The coming spectacle of Christ's judgment
english: But what a show is already near at hand: the coming of the Lord, now no longer doubted, now glorious, now triumphant! What exultation among the angels, what glory for the saints as they rise again! What a kingdom of the righteous will follow! What a city, the new Jerusalem! But there are still other shows to come: that last and everlasting day of judgment, unhoped for by the nations, the day they mocked, when all this world's great age and all its births will be consumed by one fire. What a vast spectacle that will be! What should I marvel at? What should I laugh at? Where should I rejoice, where should I exult, as I watch so many kings who were announced as received into heaven, groaning in the deepest darkness with Jupiter himself and with their own witnesses? And the governors, persecutors of the Lord's name, melting away amid flames more savage than those with which they themselves raged against the Christians? Who else? Those wise philosophers, blushing before their own disciples as they burn together with them—the ones who taught that nothing pertains to God, who insisted that souls are either nothing or will not return to their former bodies? And the poets, trembling not before the judgment seat of Rhadamanthus or Minos, but before the tribunal of the Christ they did not expect? Then the tragedians will be worth hearing, far more vocal in their own calamity; then the actors will be worth watching, much more loosened by the fire; then the charioteer will be worth seeing, all red on his flaming wheel; then the xystici will be worth contemplating, not in their gymnasiums but in the fire, hurled—except that I would not even then wish to look at them, since I would rather fix an insatiable gaze on those who raged against the Lord. This is he, I will say to the persecutors, whom you called the son of a carpenter or of a prostitute, the destroyer of the Sabbath, the Samaritan who is possessed by a demon; this is the one you redeemed from the Jews; this is the one beaten with a reed and with blows, disgraced with spittle, given gall and vinegar to drink; this is the one his disciples secretly stole away so that he could be said to have risen, the one the gardener dragged away so that his lettuces might not be damaged by the crowd of people passing through. What praetor or consul or quaestor or priest will grant you from his own generosity the chance to see such things, to exult in such things? And yet we already have these things in some way, represented through faith as the spirit imagines them. But what are those things which no eye has seen and no ear has heard, nor have they ascended into the heart of man (1 Corinthians 2:9)? I believe they are more delightful than the circus and both tiers of seats and every stadium.
orientation: Tertullian is closing the treatise by contrasting the shows of this world with the far greater spectacle of Christ's return and final judgment, which Christians already possess in part through faith.
